repo.description: A local emulator for AWS services, built and maintained by autonomous AI agents.

lead_time_hours.basis: pull request opened to the next release

change_failure_rate.basis: merged changes that are reverts or hotfixes

time_to_restore_hours.basis: issues labelled as incidents, opened to closed

checks.title: CI checks every pull request
checks.evidence: 1 workflow run on pull requests: CI
checks.why: Changes are built and tested before they merge, by people and agents alike. Agents need this most: CI is how their work gets checked.

checks.title: Tests exist and CI runs them
checks.evidence: 412 test files among 3184 files (13%); tests run in CI, Conformance
checks.why: Tests turn "it builds" into "it works". Without them, a green check says little, and agents cannot tell whether a fix fixed anything.

checks.title: The default branch is protected
checks.evidence: main is protected, with required status checks
checks.why: Nothing reaches the default branch without passing CI. It also makes auto-merging dependency updates safe, since they merge only once checks pass.

checks.title: CI on the default branch stays green
checks.evidence: 86% of 49 runs passed in 30 days; failing now: Conformance
checks.why: A default branch that is often red hides new breakages, and every agent or person branching from it starts from broken code.
checks.recommendation: Fix failures on the default branch first. Required checks on pull requests stop most of them from landing.

checks.title: Dependencies are locked
checks.evidence: 2 lock files committed
checks.why: A committed lock file makes every build install exactly what was tested, and lets scanners see the full dependency tree.

checks.title: Dependencies are updated automatically
checks.evidence: No Dependabot or Renovate configuration
checks.why: Known vulnerabilities are patched in days rather than months, and in small steps that are easy to review. Grouping minor and patch updates keeps the noise down.
checks.recommendation: Add Dependabot version updates for every ecosystem in the repository, including the GitHub Actions you use.

fixes.content:
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: cargo
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    groups:
      minor-and-patch:
        update-types: [minor, patch]
  - package-ecosystem: pip
    directory: /tests
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    groups:
      minor-and-patch:
        update-types: [minor, patch]
  - package-ecosystem: docker
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    groups:
      minor-and-patch:
        update-types: [minor, patch]
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    groups:
      minor-and-patch:
        update-types: [minor, patch]

checks.title: Patch updates merge themselves once CI passes
checks.evidence: Dependency pull requests wait for someone to merge them
checks.why: Security and patch releases land without anyone having to click merge, while your required checks still have the last word.
checks.recommendation: Turn on "Allow auto-merge" in Settings → General, require CI in a branch rule, then add this workflow. It approves and auto-merges patch and minor updates; major versions still wait for a person.

fixes.content:
name: Dependabot auto-merge
on: pull_request
permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write
jobs:
  auto-merge:
    if: github.event.pull_request.user.login == 'dependabot[bot]'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: meta
        uses: dependabot/fetch-metadata@v2
      - if: steps.meta.outputs.update-type != 'version-update:semver-major'
        run: |
          gh pr review --approve "$PR"
          gh pr merge --auto --squash "$PR"
        env:
          PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.html_url }}
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

checks.title: New dependencies are screened for malware
checks.evidence: No supply-chain scanner on pull requests
checks.why: Vulnerability databases only know about published CVEs. Supply-chain scanners like Socket read what a new package actually does (install scripts, network access, obfuscated code, typosquats) before it is merged. This matters more now that agents add dependencies.
checks.recommendation: Install the Socket GitHub App (free for open source) so it comments on pull requests that add risky packages, and add a socket.yml to tune it. Or run the Socket CLI in CI with an API token stored as a repository secret.

fixes.content:
version: 2
# Comment on pull requests that add or change dependencies.
githubApp:
  enabled: true
  dependencyOverviewEnabled: true

checks.title: Pull requests are blocked from adding vulnerable dependencies
checks.evidence: Nothing checks the dependencies a pull request adds
checks.why: Stops a pull request from introducing a dependency with a known vulnerability or a licence you do not accept.
checks.recommendation: Add the dependency review action to pull requests.

fixes.content:
name: Dependency review
on: pull_request
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/dependency-review-action@v4
        with:
          fail-on-severity: high
          comment-summary-in-pr: on-failure

checks.title: Code is scanned for vulnerabilities
checks.evidence: No code scanning workflow (CodeQL supports python, javascript-typescript)
checks.why: Finds injection, path traversal and other flaws in your own code, on every pull request. AI tools now find exploitable bugs quickly, so assume attackers do too.
checks.recommendation: Turn on CodeQL default setup in Settings → Code security, or add the workflow for more control.

fixes.content:
name: CodeQL
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: '23 4 * * 1'
permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write
jobs:
  analyze:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        language: [python, javascript-typescript]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: github/codeql-action/init@v3
        with:
          languages: ${{ matrix.language }}
          build-mode: none
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3

checks.title: OpenSSF Scorecard runs
checks.evidence: No OpenSSF Scorecard workflow
checks.why: An independent score of your security practices that users of your project can check, published as a badge.
checks.recommendation: Add the Scorecard action, weekly and on pushes to the default branch.

fixes.content:
name: Scorecard
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: '41 5 * * 2'
permissions: read-all
jobs:
  analysis:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      security-events: write
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: ossf/scorecard-action@v2
        with:
          results_file: results.sarif
          results_format: sarif
          publish_results: true
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: results.sarif

checks.title: Actions are pinned to a commit
checks.evidence: 6 action references use a tag or branch, which its owner can move
checks.why: A tag can be moved to malicious code, as in the tj-actions/changed-files compromise. A commit SHA cannot, and Dependabot still keeps pinned actions up to date.
checks.recommendation: Pin each action to the SHA of its release, with the version in a comment. A tool such as pin-github-action does it for you; Dependabot's github-actions ecosystem then keeps the pins current.

fixes.content:
npx pin-github-action .github/workflows/*.yml
# uses: actions/checkout@v4  becomes
# uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4

checks.title: Workflows ask for least privilege
checks.evidence: 2 workflows without a permissions block: conformance.yml, release.yml
checks.why: If a step is compromised, a read-only token limits what it can do. Without a permissions block, the token gets the repository default, which may allow writes.
checks.recommendation: Add a top-level permissions block to each workflow, starting from contents: read, and grant more only to the jobs that need it.

checks.title: There is a way to report vulnerabilities privately
checks.evidence: Policy in SECURITY.md
checks.why: Researchers, and the AI tools that now find exploits, need a private route to report them. Otherwise reports arrive as public issues, or not at all.

checks.title: Code has owners
checks.evidence: No CODEOWNERS file
checks.why: Each change, whether from a person or an agent, is routed to someone accountable for that part of the code. A branch rule can require their review.
checks.recommendation: Add a CODEOWNERS file, starting with a default owner.

fixes.content:
# Default owner for everything.
*       @aws

# Workflows and security settings.
/.github/  @aws

checks.title: Issue forms
checks.evidence: 2 issue forms: behavior-differs.yml, feature-request.yml
checks.why: Forms keep reports complete, and each form labels its issues. That lets the dashboard tell bugs from feature requests and apply the right time limit.

checks.title: Issues are labelled
checks.evidence: 1% of 510 issues carry a label
checks.why: Labels separate bugs, security reports and feature requests, each with its own time limit. Incident labels feed time to restore.
checks.recommendation: Label every issue at triage, at least bug or enhancement. Issue forms do it for you.

checks.title: Closed issues link to their fix
checks.evidence: 10% of 41 completed closures reference a commit, pull request or release
checks.why: A closure that links to its fix can be verified. Without the link, nobody can tell a fixed issue from one that was closed and forgotten.
checks.recommendation: Close issues from the fix: write "Fixes #123" in the pull request description. GitHub closes the issue when the change merges and records the link.

checks.title: Pull request template
checks.evidence: No pull request template
checks.why: A template prompts every author, person or agent, to link the issue, say how it was tested and credit an agent.
checks.recommendation: Add a short pull request template.

fixes.content:
## What and why

Fixes #

## How it was tested

## AI assistance

<!-- Name any coding agent that helped, or keep its Co-Authored-By trailer. -->

checks.title: Deliveries are recorded
checks.evidence: 9 releases published
checks.why: Deployment frequency and lead time measure delivery to users, not merges. Releases or GitHub deployments give the dashboard the real dates.

checks.title: Incidents are labelled
checks.evidence: 2 issues labelled as incidents
checks.why: Time to restore service is measured from incident issues. Without the label it cannot be measured at all.

checks.title: Agents have instructions
checks.evidence: Instructions in AGENTS.md
checks.why: Coding agents read these files before they work. Telling them how to build, test and attribute their work makes their pull requests mergeable first time.

checks.title: Agent work is attributed
checks.evidence: 32 of 58 pull requests in 30 days show an agent's work
checks.why: Agent work through people's accounts looks human unless it is attributed. Without that, the dashboard undercounts what agents contribute.

checks.title: An agent helps run the project
checks.evidence: No agent runs in the repository's workflows
checks.why: An agent in Actions can triage and label new issues, answer questions, and act on what this dashboard finds, all inside GitHub. Its API key stays a repository secret. It must never go in the dashboard, which is a public page.
checks.recommendation: Store your API key as the repository secret ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions) and add a triage workflow. Mention @claude in an issue or pull request for anything else.

fixes.content:
name: Agent triage
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
permissions:
  contents: read
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  triage:
    if: github.event_name == 'issues' || contains(github.event.comment.body, '@claude')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          prompt: |
            For a new issue: label it bug, enhancement, security or question,
            ask for anything a bug report is missing, and link duplicates.
            Read the repository's dashboard data in the gh-pages branch
            (dashboard/data/status.json) for open issues past their limits.

checks.title: The dashboard can read everything it measures
checks.evidence: Every read succeeded
checks.why: Delivery and CI figures need read access to Actions runs and deployments. The Action never writes anywhere but the Pages branch.

checks.title: The dashboard updates on a schedule
checks.evidence: Runs every 6 hours
checks.why: Fresh data, and a history with no gaps for the forecast to learn from.

checks.title: Costs are set
checks.evidence: No prices set, so the outlook has no cost figures
checks.why: With prices set, the outlook shows what resolving issues costs a month, people against agents, and when keeping pace would exceed a budget.
checks.recommendation: Set what an agent costs per resolved issue (your API spend divided by the issues agents resolved), a person's hourly rate, and a monthly budget.

fixes.content:
- uses: sholtomaud/repo-sre-dashboard@v1
  with:
    agent-cost-per-issue: '1.50'   # API spend ÷ issues agents resolved
    human-hourly-rate: '95'
    human-hours-per-issue: '2'
    monthly-budget: '5000'
    currency: USD

checks.title: README, licence and contributing guide
checks.evidence: All present
checks.why: Contributors and agents learn how to build, test and send changes. A licence says whether anyone may use the code at all.
